About: The Damped Oscillator — Under, Over, and Critical

Source

Lecture
Classical mechanics — oscillations: the free damped oscillator, ẍ + 2αẋ + ω₀²x = 0.
Simulation
Spring-mass released from x₀ = 1 m with a live x–t trace; a one-mass explore mode plus a counterfactual three-lane settle race (α = 0.6 / 3 / 6 rad/s).
Concept
Damping speeds the return to rest only up to α = ω₀; past critical, the slow root α − √(α²−ω₀²) makes the mass crawl back.
Serves
Regime classification (underdamped / critical / overdamped); exact closed-form solutions in all three regimes; the non-monotonic settling-rate peak λ_max = ω₀ at α = ω₀.
Inquiry
Before dragging, predict which reaches rest first — the critical mass or the most heavily damped — then run the race and watch the decay-rate readout climb to its peak at critical and drop past it.
Misconception
"More damping always settles faster" — past critical the mass returns SLOWER; the fastest non-oscillatory return is at α = ω₀ exactly.
Decay-rate map
λ(α) = α − √(max(0, α² − ω₀²)) — the rate of the slowest surviving exponential. The white dot on the map tracks your slider’s α.

The Damped Oscillator
⚠ RACE predict — first to rest:

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict — which reaches rest first?

Three identical spring–mass systems, each released from x₀ = 1 m at rest, differing only in their damping α = 0.60, 3 and 6 rad/s. The spring's natural frequency is ω₀ = 3 rad/s. Which one reaches rest first — inside the ±2 cm band, and staying?

2 · The race

The three masses are released together. Each lane plants a flag at the instant it enters the ±2 cm band for good. Watch how long α = 6 keeps crawling after α = 3 has finished.

3 · The underdamped case

One mass now, with α = 0.60 rad/s — well below ω₀ = 3. It is released from a height of x₀ = 1 m. Will it cross the x = 0 reference line, or go to rest without ever reaching it?

4 · Critical damping

The damping factor is now critical, α = ω₀ = 3 rad/s. Compare the trace with the underdamped case: how many times does it cross x = 0?

5 · The overdamped case

Now observe the overdamped case, α = 6 rad/s — twice ω₀. How is its return to rest different from the critically damped case?

6 · λ peaks at α = ω₀

The decay-rate map plots λ(α), the rate of the slowest surviving exponential: λ = α below critical, λ = α − √(α² − ω₀²) above it. It climbs to its maximum λ = ω₀ = 3 rad/s exactly at α = ω₀ and falls away after — which is why damping past critical returns the mass more slowly, not faster.

The Damped Oscillator

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A mass on a spring loses energy to friction, and the damping α decides how it comes back to rest. The sim draws the exact motion for any α, and it can release three masses with different damping together.

What you'll learn

  • How the damping α, compared with the spring's own rate ω₀, sets the kind of motion.
  • What the decay rate λ means, and how to read it from the sim.
  • What fixes the time a damped mass takes to reach rest, and how α changes it.
A mass on a spring with a damper, held 1 m above equilibrium and released from rest.

What's on screen

  • One mass: the mass on its spring, with a trace of its height x against time. The mass and the trace head sit at the same height.
  • Settle race: three masses side by side, with α = 0.60, 3 and the slider value (6 on entry).
  • Green band: |x| ≤ 2 cm, the sim's meaning of at rest. A ✓ at rest flag marks when a mass enters it for good.
  • Decay rate λ readout and the decay-rate map λ(α), with a white dot at your α.
See itHold one mass at its release height. Watch for: a violet mass at x = +1 m, above the dashed x = 0 line.

03

Damping α, set against ω₀, sorts the motion into three kinds

The sim solves one equation. Here ω₀² = k/m, so ω₀ = 3 rad/s, and 2α = b/m, where b is the drag coefficient.

ẍ + 2αẋ + ω₀² x = 0
Mass on a spring with damping. Start: x = x₀ = 1 m, ẋ = 0.

The solutions are built from ert, where r = −α ± √(α² − ω₀²). The sign inside the square root sorts the motion.

dampingroots rname
α < ω₀a complex pairunderdamped
α = ω₀one repeated real root, −ω₀critical
α > ω₀two different real rootsoverdamped
Key idea. What matters is α compared with ω₀, never α alone.
04

An underdamped mass rings inside a shrinking envelope

x = x₀ e−αt ( cos ωdt + (α/ωd) sin ωdt )
For α < ω₀, with ωd = √(ω₀² − α²).
  • The mass oscillates at ωd, a little below ω₀. At α = 0.60, ωd = 2.94 rad/s, so one swing takes 2.14 s.
  • The factor e−αt is the envelope. It shrinks every swing, and the mass crosses x = 0 on each half swing.
  • At α = 0.60 the first low point is x = −0.53 m, at t = 1.07 s.
  • The envelope reaches 2 cm when e−αt = 0.02, at t = ln 50 / α = 6.52 s. The sim's flag reads 6.53 s.
See itRelease one mass with α = 0.60. Watch for: the trace crossing the dashed x = 0 line, with each swing smaller than the last.
05

Critical and overdamped motion return without crossing x = 0

  • Critical, α = ω₀. x = x₀(1 + ω₀t) e−ω₀t. The mass is released from rest, falls to x = 0, and never goes below it.
  • Overdamped, α > ω₀. x is a sum of two decaying exponentials, one for each real root. Released from rest, the mass again stays above x = 0.
  • At α = 6 the roots are −0.80 and −11.2 rad/s. The fast term is gone after about 0.1 s. The slow root carries the rest of the return.

So the three kinds differ in more than speed. Only the underdamped mass crosses the equilibrium line.

See itRelease one mass with α = ω₀ = 3 rad/s. Watch for: the trace sliding down to the x = 0 line without crossing it.
06

The slowest decay rate λ peaks at α = ω₀

For large t, the motion decays as e−λt, where λ is the smaller magnitude of the roots.

λ = α (α ≤ ω₀), λ = α − √(α² − ω₀²) (α > ω₀)
The Decay rate λ readout, in rad/s.
  • λ rises with slope 1 up to α = ω₀, where λ = ω₀ = 3 rad/s. Then it falls.
  • The two roots multiply to ω₀². Extra friction pushes the fast root out and pulls the slow root in.
  • At α = 3.05 the sim shows λ = 2.50 rad/s, and at α = 6 only 0.80 rad/s. The same λ = 1.00 rad/s occurs at α = 1 and α = 5.
See itOpen the decay-rate map at α = 3 rad/s. Watch for: the white dot on the top of the λ(α) curve, with λ = 3.00 rad/s.
07

Critical damping reaches rest first of the three masses

Settle race starts all three masses at x₀ = 1 m. A mass is at rest when |x| ≤ 2 cm and stays there.

damping (rad/s)kindat rest after
0.60underdamped6.53 s
3critical1.94 s
6overdamped4.96 s
  • The underdamped mass keeps crossing x = 0 until its swings shrink inside 2 cm.
  • The overdamped mass has no ringing, but its slow rate λ = 0.80 rad/s leaves a long tail.

This ranking is for these three lanes. For this band, the shortest time overall is at α ≈ 2.35 (slightly underdamped), 1.21 s. Critical damping has the largest λ and the quickest return that never crosses x = 0.

See itRelease all three masses together. Watch for: three ✓ at rest flags on the chart, at 1.94 s, 4.96 s and 6.53 s.
08

Where it matters

  • Moving-coil meters. A galvanometer pointer is damped near critical, so it settles on the reading without swinging back and forth.
  • Car shock absorbers. They damp the bounce of the suspension springs. Most are set below critical damping, which allows a small overshoot for a softer ride.
  • Door closers. A closer is set near critical damping, so the door shuts without slamming or creeping.
09

Summary

In one line. The damping α, compared with the spring's own rate ω₀, decides how the mass returns to rest. This sim lets you vary α and measure the time to reach rest.

Key points

  • The equation ẍ + 2αẋ + ω₀² x = 0 gives underdamped (α < ω₀), critical (α = ω₀) and overdamped (α > ω₀) motion.
  • Only an underdamped mass crosses x = 0 after release from rest.
  • The slowest decay rate λ peaks at ω₀, where α = ω₀.
  • Past α = ω₀, more damping makes the return slower, because the slow root shrinks.

Common mix-ups

  • "More damping always brings the mass to rest sooner." Past α = ω₀ it slows the return. At α = 6 it takes 4.96 s, against 1.94 s at α = 3.
  • "Underdamped means almost no damping." The mass loses energy all the time. Its swings shrink as e−αt.
  • "Critical damping is the fastest way into any at-rest band." It has the largest λ. A slightly smaller α enters this ±2 cm band sooner.

Things to try on your own

  • Set α = 1, then α = 5, and compare the Decay rate λ readouts and the shape of the two traces.
  • Step the slider from 3.00 to 3.05 and note how far λ drops.
